## Thesis Organization and Chapter Overview

The thesis proceeds from problem formulation and motivating literature to agent design and implementation, and finally to empirical evaluation.

Chapter I introduces the problem context, defines the research scope, and
presents the methodological framework used throughout the thesis.

Chapter II reviews the literature most directly relevant to the present research
question. It covers market microstructure evidence motivating order-book-derived
features, the landscape of alternative machine learning paradigms and trading
decision architectures, the structural case for reinforcement learning in
trading, and prior RL trading applications with attention to action-space
design, transaction-cost modeling, and evaluation rigor.

Chapter III develops the reinforcement learning foundations required for the
thesis, with particular emphasis on the progression from earlier methods to TD3
and on the distinctions that matter for continuous-control trading problems.

Chapter IV presents the design of the trading agent itself. It defines the
continuous action space, the microstructure-aware state representation, the
reward formulation, and the main policy and value-function design choices used
in the empirical system.

Chapter V describes the implementation of the research pipeline, including the
simulation architecture, data preparation, reproducible feature engineering,
code structure, and the TD3-based training workflow used to produce
reproducible experiments.

Chapter VI reports the empirical results. It combines experiment snapshots,
performance evaluation, statistical validation, and robustness assessment to
separate promising outcomes from noise, overfitting, or fragile conclusions.

Chapter VII synthesizes the findings, discusses the main limitations of the
current framework, and draws implications for future research and practical
trading-system development.

Accompanying these chapters is the codebase that produced every result reported
in them, released as an open repository [@Wojdalski2026]. It is an inherent part
of the work rather than supporting material: the pipeline described in Chapter V,
the scenario configurations defining each hypothesis test in Chapter VI, and the
evaluation and statistical-testing code behind every reported figure all reside
there. Experiments are specified declaratively, so each scenario compared in
Chapters 6 and 7 can be re-run from its configuration file without modifying
source code. This matters for more than convenience. Several claims the thesis
makes about its own method are properties of the implementation: that feature
normalization uses only past observations, that splits are chronological, that
the scenarios of each hypothesis differ in one factor at a time. The repository is
what makes them auditable rather than merely asserted.
